headlines.article_text: Elon Musk's SpaceX gift: How Trump Account rules could apply Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Elon Musk posted on X that he will give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year. The world's richest person appeared to suggest that he would use the Trump Account program to make this historic gift. Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT SpaceX CEO Elon Musk speaks to reporters as President Donald Trump looks on outside the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026. Tierney L. Cross | The Washington Post | Getty Images Elon Musk said on Monday that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. He appeared to suggest the gift could land in Trump Accounts — thanking Brad Gerstner, an architect of the program, for "helping enable this" in a comment on X . But if the shares are distributed through the new investment accounts for children, the gift could come with significant strings attached. Musk's announcement comes weeks after the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out guidelines for stock donations to Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts. Those include restrictions on selling donated stock: Children who receive it generally cannot sell for five years, even if the company runs into financial trouble. Treasury's temporary regulations, subject to revision after public comment, aim to encourage stock gifts. But they also give donors unusual influence over children's investments, according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. Under the new Trump Account rules, however, it's "the donor that's dictating the terms of the gift," she said. Representatives for Musk, Gerstner and the Treasury Department did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment on the proposed gift. According to the Treasury, about 70 million Trump Accounts have been created, including more than 60 million through a recent auto-enrollment effort . Trump Accounts are available to all children with U.S. citizenship under age 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Musk would be the second philanthropist to publicly announce a stock pledge to Trump Accounts: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell pledged earlier this summer to use the Trump Account program to gift some 2 million shares . That gift has not yet been distributed. What stock sale restrictions mean for children Trump Account beneficiaries do not have the latitude to sell under circumstances that other investors might otherwise. Under the new rules, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17. Before then, early sales are permitted only in limited circumstances, such as certain corporate transitions or when the stock is formally delisted from a national securities exchange — not when financial or legal problems emerge that might prompt an investor to sell. "Giving families more choices and more ability to hold the assets that they think are best for them and their kids' future ... would be a good thing," said Adam Michel, director of tax policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. "But this is not really that, because you have no choice in the asset that is being deposited into your child's account, and then you also have no ability to sell it for the five-year holding period." watch now VIDEO 1:53 01:53 Elon Musk vows to donate SpaceX shares to every child in America The Exchange The temporary regulations also mandate that if any gifted stock is sold too early, the trustee must purchase the same number and class of shares "as soon as practicable." This increases beneficiaries' risk of loss if the share price rises before the trustee repurchases the stock, according to Schenck. Beneficiaries would ultimately bear that cost. "If the fiduciary makes an investment mistake, then the focus is typically restoring value to the beneficiary. But here, the focus seems to be restoring the specific security itself," said Schenck, who left the IRS in 2025 for law firm Caplin & Drysdale. CNBC has learned the buyback provision is intended to quickly correct trading errors, though the regulations do not explicitly state that purpose or limit the requirement to accidental sales. Donor incentives behind the holding rule The temporary regulations cite donor interests. According to the text, "Donors are attracted by the hope that a stock contribution with a five-year holding period may lead recipients and their families to feel that they have a stake in the fate of the corporation." Restricting sales virtually eliminates the risk for donors and their companies that Trump Account recipients will sell gifted shares en masse, liquidating a large enough position to depress share prices, according to Jane Ditelberg, chief tax strategist at Northern Trust. "Certainly, for people who have highly concentrated wealth in a company, and the assets are sitting in their own personal pockets, this makes it a lot easier to give," she said. "The major donors we've engaged are motivated by a desire to help children build generational wealth and get a head start on their financial future," the official said in a written statement. Treasury has said it is in discussions with Trump Accounts donors ranging from "small to mega," but has not identified additional stock pledges since Shotwell's July announcement. CNBC has identified fewer than a dozen pledges from philanthropists, though about four dozen major employers have committed to seed accounts for their employees' children. In documents explaining the temporary rules, Treasury pointed to Michael and Susan Dell's $6.25 billion cash pledge and unspecified "similar donations," while acknowledging uncertainty about whether that level of giving will continue. "It is unclear whether this level of giving can be sustained in the long run or whether it is concentrated as Trump accounts are launching," the text states. Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG consensus estimates: Revenue: $12.72 billion expected Earnings per share: 13 cents expected While SpaceX is best known for its reusable rockets, most of its revenue and profit in recent quarters came from the company's connectivity segment, which consists of its Starlink satellite internet service. Buzz is building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. mobile network after SpaceX, earlier this month, announced that it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation. The moves strengthen "Starlink Mobile's ability to compete with major carriers by enabling broader, deeper coverage," RBC Capital Markets analysts wrote in a note ahead of earnings. The firm has a $225 price target on SpaceX stock and the equivalent of a buy rating. In the third quarter, analysts are expecting AI revenue of $6.47 billion, connectivity sales of $4.84 billion, and revenue in the space business of $1.41 billion, according to StreetAccount. During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor. What you need to know ahead of the earnings report: Capex and AI data center expansion Here's why analysts are bullish on SpaceX heading into the report Tesla-SpaceX merger speculation 53 Min Ago Tough time for neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius in October SpaceX is relatively new to the cloud computing business. Many of its competitors in the space, the so-called neoclouds, have been getting hammered on Wall Street of late on concerns that rising interest rates are going to make the costly buildout financially burdensome. CoreWeave and Nebius are down 28% so far in October, while IREN has plunged about 35%. Earlier this month, Australian AI data center operator Firmus withdrew its planned IPO, citing market volatility and conditions. While SpaceX is far less reliant on that side of its business than are the neoclouds, capital costs still matter, and the company is banking on the AI boom continuing. In the second quarter, debt and finance leases increased to $36.8 billion, up from $22 billion the prior period. —Ari Levy 2 Hours Ago How the stock has done since the IPO Billboards in Times Square celebrate the SpaceX IPO debut at the Nasdaq on June 12th, 2026. Adam Jeffery | CNBC SpaceX stock chart. Since opening at $150 on June 12, SpaceX shares have edged slightly lower, slipping to $147.50 on Tuesday. That gives Space a market cap of about $2 trillion. The stock hit a low of $104.83 on Aug. 3, a few days before the first post-IPO lockup expired, making more than 911 million SpaceX shares available for trading. The lockup lifted on Aug. 6, and the stock rallied, popping 6% initially, then nearly 16% the day after. —Lora Kolodny 2 Hours Ago Starship hits several milestones, but is still being tested The SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy v3 Booster lift off on its 14th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, US, September 28, 2026. Steve Nesius | Reuters SpaceX continues to serve as a critical launch provider to the U.S. Defense Department and NASA. The business hasn't been historically profitable, but it's the segment that captured the public's interest in the rocket maker. In the second quarter, SpaceX reported launch revenue of $962 million and a net loss of $542 million. Future profitability hinges on the success of SpaceX's Starship mega-rocket, which is still being developed and tested. Since the company's last earnings call in August, SpaceX hit multiple milestones, reaching orbit and using Starship to deploy dozens of its new V.3 Starlink satellites during Test Flight 14. But the rocket is still far from reliable or reusable. Investors are awaiting an update on pending NASA missions and the future of the older Falcon rocket. SpaceX has reportedly stopped allowing other companies to launch their cargo, including satellites, into orbit on Falcon missions. —Lora Kolodny 3 Hours Ago Capex and the SpaceXAI data center build out A drone view shows the xAI Colossus 2 "Macrohard" data centre in Southaven, Mississippi, U.S., May 30, 2026. Kevin Wurm | Reuters In its first earnings report in August, SpaceX reported capital expenditures of $18.4 billion, with 80% of that going towards its artificial intelligence division. That number spooked Wall Street, and shares dropped following the report. SpaceX and xAI merged in February and the company has been pouring money into its effort to become a major player in AI, a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The AI division also acquired Cursor in a $60 billion transaction and is now known as either SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI, with the "SI" standing for President Donald Trump's preferred "Super Intelligence." — Lora Kolodny 4 Hours Ago Analysts are bullish on SpaceX ahead of earnings A general view of a SpaceX building on the day of the company’s initial public offering (IPO), in Starbase, Texas, U.S., June 12, 2026. Gabriel V. Cardenas | Reuters Wall Street is sounding bullish on SpaceX ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, to be delivered after the bell on Tuesday. Analysts are expecting some conversation about deals or competitive plays with cable and telecom companies following SpaceX's acquisition of low-band spectrum earlier this month. "We expect initial strategic commentary centers around Connectivity and how SPCX can partner/compete its way into global markets, although we think low-band distribution becomes a meaningful intelligence lever over time," Colin Canfield at Cantor Fitzgerald wrote in a Monday note. He has a price target of $246 and an overweight rating on the stock. Oppenheimer's expectations are more measured. The bank thinks the quarter will be "in-line" with "guidance reiterated." "Industry subscriber growth is slowing with limited room for pricing action, so focus is shifting from net adds and service revenue growth toward cost-cutting using AI, and lower subsidies/churn," Timothy Horan at Oppenheimer told clients in a Tuesday note.
